The first thing I bought for my apartment was a table that would not fit through the door. I had measured the wall where it would stand and the space between the radiator and the window. I had even measured my knees while sitting down. The door, which I used twice every day, had escaped my attention. For forty minutes the table stood on the landing like a large animal declining to enter a trailer. My neighbor came home with groceries, considered the situation, and said, “Have you tried taking the legs off?” We became friends, although not immediately on equal terms.

His name was Martin. He owned tools in the casual way other people own teaspoons. If you needed something to grip a pipe without scratching it, he went into his kitchen and returned with exactly that. His kitchen drawers contained very little cutlery. Once, eating soup at his place, I asked for a second spoon, and he handed me a measuring spoon marked one tablespoon. It worked perfectly well, except that I became unpleasantly aware of how much soup I was eating. Martin finished first and rinsed his bowl. “Twenty-three,” I told him. He nodded as if this confirmed his estimate.

After we got the table inside, I spent a week trying to decide what to put on it. In the furniture shop it had held a blue jug, three lemons, and a book about Portugal. At home it held my keys, a gas bill, and the small wrench Martin had forgotten. I bought lemons. Within a few days I had used one for fish and one for tea, and the remaining lemon looked less like a decision than an oversight. The jug never materialized. The wrench stayed. It was the one thing on the table that visitors consistently picked up.

My sister came over to help me paint. We covered the table with newspaper and set the open tin in the middle. Halfway through the afternoon she sat down, still holding her brush, to tell me that she was thinking of leaving her job. She had been thinking about it for months. While she talked, a drop of green paint traveled down the handle, crossed her knuckle, and landed beyond the edge of the newspaper. Neither of us noticed until later. She apologized and tried to lift it with a fingernail. I said to leave it. She left the job in June.

I would like to say that, whenever I saw the green mark, I thought of her courage. Usually I thought it was a pea. Several times I tried to brush it onto the floor. Objects are unreliable custodians of the meanings we assign them. They keep the evidence and decline to supply the story. Someone buying that table secondhand might reasonably conclude that its former owner painted carelessly or ate vegetables without enthusiasm. They would never guess that my sister had stood beside it, wiping her hands on her trousers, practicing what she would say to her boss on Monday morning.

In winter Martin started coming downstairs on Thursdays to do the crossword. His apartment was warmer, but mine had the better light. We made rules. No looking anything up before eight. No writing an answer unless you could explain it. Proper names were exempt from the second rule because neither of us could explain why we knew the names of racehorses. We ate toast over the puzzle and accumulated crumbs in the fold. Now and then a clue defeated us for weeks afterward. We could remember the question exactly but not the number of letters, which made further thought essentially useless.

One Thursday he brought down a letter from his daughter. She wanted him to move closer to her. There was a flat available near the station, with a lift and a small balcony. We examined the photographs on his phone. The balcony faced a brick wall, but if you leaned out, his daughter had written, you could see a chestnut tree. Martin enlarged the photograph until the supposed tree dissolved into green squares. “Could be anybody’s tree,” he said. We did the crossword. At half past eight he said he had already paid the deposit. I put the kettle on again.

When he moved, he gave me the contents of one kitchen drawer. There were pliers, washers, two screwdrivers, and a little brass key that he could not identify. I offered him his wrench back. He seemed surprised to see it. “That’s yours,” he said, with the mild impatience of a man correcting an error in arithmetic. I put it with the other tools. They filled the drawer in my kitchen where I had been keeping takeaway menus. For months afterward I opened it expecting the number of a curry house and encountered instead the means to tighten a tap.

Several years later, when I moved out, my sister helped me carry the table downstairs. We took the legs off first. On the underside, written in pencil, was a name neither of us recognized, followed by a date some thirty years before I bought it. Beside the name someone had drawn a fish with surprisingly human teeth. My sister took a photograph. I wondered who had drawn it and whether the person signing the table had approved. Then we heard the van driver sounding his horn, and the fish went facedown against a blanket, keeping its expression to itself.

The table stands in my kitchen now. On Thursday evenings Martin sometimes calls with a clue. His daughter has bought him a book of difficult puzzles, and he suspects the compiler of making mistakes. While we talk, I clear a space among the envelopes and cups and write his suggestions on whatever comes to hand. Last week the answer was “wobble.” I sat back, pleased, and felt the table shift under my elbow. One leg needed tightening. I knew which drawer to open. Martin waited on the line while I knelt beneath the table, eye to eye with the fish.
